newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: U.S. evacuates more foreigners from Sierra Leone.
newsitem.headline: U.S. evacuates more foreigners from Sierra Leone.

text.p: held)
By John Chiahemen

U.S. helicopters began a fresh evacuation of foreign nationals from Sierra Leone's beleaguered capital on Tuesday. Coup leaders said they were using 300 Nigerian soldiers as human shields against air attack.
Nigeria, acting in the name of Sierra Leone's West African neighbours to reinstate the former British colony's civilian president, flew in reinforcements from Liberia.

The coup leaders, who announced on national radio that the 300 Nigerians soldiers had surrendered, put the death toll in a Nigerian naval gunboat bombardment and associated fighting on Monday at 80. Hospital sources said it was at least 62.
Officials in Lagos said they had no information on Nigerian soldiers being held hostage or used as human shields.
Witnesses and residents said that the city itself was calm. Some reported shops were open in some parts of town and street traders were hawking their wares.

Nigerian forces, who suffered a setback on Monday, are intervening in the name of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) which has a Nigerian-led peacekeeping force called ECOMOG in neighbouring Liberia.
They agreed a ceasefire with the coup leaders after Monday's initial strike failed to force them and their rebel allies to step down and reinstate ousted president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.

"We agreed a ceasefire yesterday. We hope they will respect it because if not, we are building the capacity to carry on the offensive," ECOMOG's Nigerian field commander, General Victor Malu, told Reuters.

Dissident Sierra Leonean soldiers and their allies from the rebel Revolutionary United Front set up roadblocks after clashing with Nigerian soldiers on Monday around the beachfront Mammy Yoko hotel, following the naval bombardment.

U.S. helicopters resumed an air shuttle of foreign nationals from the city. Britain strongly urged its nationals to take advantage of Tuesday's airlift, saying no more attempts would be made to get people out.
An airlift last week ferried out more than 1,255 Americans, foreigners and some deposed government officials.
"We began another phase of the evacuation from Freetown," a U.S. Defence Department spokeswoman said in Washington. She predicted the operation would end in a few hours.
CH-53 Sea Stallion helicopters, which can carry up to 55 passengers, and CH-46 Sea Knight helicopters, capable of carrying 22 passengers, were being used.
Evacuees have previously been taken to the nearby warship, the USS Kearsarge, and on to Guinea's capital Conakry.
Witnesses in Liberia's capital Monrovia said three more helicopters left for Freetown with dozens of heavily armed Nigerians on board. They had artillery and rocket launchers.
ECOMOG commander Malu said Nigeria would bring in jet bombers and troop reinforcements to Lungi international airport.

The International Committee of the Red Cross brokered Monday's ceasefire to allow the evacuation of more than 600 civilians trapped by fighting around the Mammy Yoko Hotel. Malu said the ceasefire was now in force city-wide.

Nigeria and Guinea, who already had ECOMOG troops in Sierra Leone, sent reinforcements after the May 25 coup. They are thought to have about 3,000 men in Freetown. Ghana said it was sending troops, but only to evacuate its nationals.
The coup leaders have accused Kabbah of failing to consolidate a peace accord signed last November with rebel leader Foday Sankoh, and of encouraging ethnic conflict.
Sankoh, named as vice-chairman in Major Johnny Paul Koromah's ruling Armed Forces Revolutionary Council on Sunday, is being held in Nigeria. He has told his men to back the coup.
